https://www.walesonline.co.uk/whats-on/s.text: A trip to the beauty salon is a luxury many of us enjoy, yet the costs can quickly mount up. The alternative — a DIY manicure at home — often falls short in terms of longevity and that coveted professional finish. Now, shoppers say they have been swapping salon appointments for a mineral bond nail set from Australian brand Sistaco, and the retailer is currently running a promotion where beauty enthusiasts can bag three extra colours completely free of charge. Usually priced at £100.95, the set is available for £75, which works out at roughly the equivalent of two salon gel manicures. The set uses a mineral bond applicator to deliver non-toxic, HEMA and TPO free results from the comfort of the buyer's own home. Those who dread the wait for nails to dry will also be relieved to know the manicure dries instantly, making smudges a thing of the past. The set has the potential to save regular salon visitors hundreds, or even thousands, of pounds on their fortnightly appointments. Users simply apply a base coat layer and set it with an LED light, brush the powder onto the nail, add a thin top coat layer, and finish by returning to the LED light once more, reports OK! If the Sistaco set doesn't appeal, LookFantastic is currently stocking the Mylee The Midi Gel Polish Kit (worth £122) for £71.10 - reduced from £79 - featuring an LED lamp, four best-selling gel polishes and more. Meanwhile, those in need of nail tools might want to consider Sephora's £19.99 Manicure Tool Kit, which includes a nail clipper, nail file, cuticle pusher and cuticle nipper. Returning to Sistaco, the brand's Mineral Bond Nail Set has earned an impressive 4.8-star rating out of five on the retailer's website. It has also garnered strong reviews on Trustpilot, where customers have awarded the company 4.5 out of five stars based on thousands of reviews. One customer said: "Those compliments keep coming. I find in restaurants or cafes the girls/ladies that serve me always compliment my nails. "Seems random strangers can't resist! They're always so impressed when I say I did them myself." Another raved: "Is this some sort of magic? ! Love this kit and how easy it is to do at home and long lasting. Just past the two week mark on the first mani and still going strong." A third said: "I really enjoy the Sistaco system for nail colour. The colours are vibrant and there are so many shades to choose from. "I find that Sistaco lasts just as long, if not longer than an expensive salon gel manicure. The process of applying the Sistaco system is simple takes far less time than a salon visit. My days of expensive salon manicures may be over." It is worth noting that one reviewer mentioned they had found doing their own nails at home slightly challenging, writing: "As a right handed novice doing my left hand was really easy, the right not so easy. I'm sure as I get more practice my right hand will get a lot better, I also love the colour." Despite this, another customer praised the durability of the products in a Trustpilot review, writing: "Sistaco is BY FAR the best system/polish that I have ever tried! I am also very conscious of toxins and love that this is non toxic!" "I also love that it last at least two weeks and can handle all the cooking, cleaning, hand washing, and childcare activities I do as a working mom!" A further reviewer on the platform commented: "Sistaco is spectacular. I've tried basic polish, gel, and dip powders, but nothing compares to Sistaco. I was hesitant to try yet another system, but I am so glad I did. "It's easy to apply, long‐lasting, and gentle on my nails. The colours are gorgeous, the products are high‐quality, and the community is incredibly friendly and supportive. I very highly recommend Sistaco Mineral Bond nail products." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qj.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Kratom is legal in some states, including Mississippi Published 3 October 2026 A father and son who worked at a Mississippi smoke shop have been arrested and charged in connection with the death of at least one university student who died from a suspected overdose of kratom, sometimes called "gas station heroin" in the US. The pair worked at a shop that allegedly sold derivatives of the substance to University of Mississippi students. US prosecutors charged Yahya Mohamed Mosleh, 51, and Islam Yahya Mosleh, 18, for possession with the intent to distribute controlled substances in connection with the death investigation of two Ole Miss students last month. Although their deaths have not officially been attributed to kratom, officials afterward issued warnings about consuming kratom . The criminal complaint alleges that on 21 September, an Ole Miss student was found dead in his dorm room. The apparent cause of death "appeared to be consistent with a drug overdose", the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi said in a press release. Law enforcement found packages - with some tablets missing - of suspected kratom derivatives. About an hour later, a second student was found dead from a suspected overdose in another location, also with packages of suspected kratom derivatives. Officials connected the packages with the local vape, tobacco and beer store, the US Attorney's statement said. Law enforcement executed search warrants and seized suspected kratom derivative controlled substances from the store. The Mosleh's, father and son, were later arrested. The two students' deaths have sparked alarm and warnings from officials about the plant-based drug referred to as "gas station heroin". Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form. For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it is illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi. The Mississippi prosecutors said that kratom derivatives, such as MGPI, MGM-15 and MGM-16, are now schedule I controlled substances in the US and can be significantly more potent than natural kratom leaf products and morphine.
